title: AbbVie Presents Data for ABBV-466, a Novel Dual-Targeting Therapy Demonstrating Higher Endoscopic Remission Rates Than Either Anti-IL-23 or Anti-α4β7 Monotherapy in Moderate to Severe Crohn's Disease
summary: In a Phase 2a study, ABBV-466 achieved higher endoscopic remission rates in patients with Crohn's disease than either anti-IL-23 p19 or anti-α4β7 monotherapy at Week 12, the primary endpoint....
body_markdown:
- *In a Phase 2a study, ABBV-466 achieved higher endoscopic remission rates in patients with Crohn's disease than either anti-IL-23 p19 or anti-α4β7 monotherapy at Week 12, the primary endpoint. The treatment difference between ABBV-466 and the monotherapy groups further increased at Week 24* *1*
- *Gene expression analysis showed that ABBV-466 treated Crohn's disease patients experienced intestinal tissue repair and barrier restoration by Week 12, with tissue remodeling and metabolic changes reported at Week 24* *1*
- *The results will be presented as a late-breaker at the 2026 Annual United European Gastroenterology Week Congress*


NORTH CHICAGO, Ill.


, Oct. 19, 2026


/[PRNewswire](http://www.prnewswire.com/) / -- AbbVie (NYSE: ABBV) today announced that its investigational ABBV-466, a novel dual-targeting therapy against IL-23 p19 and integrin α4β7, demonstrated higher rates of endoscopic remissiona at Week 12 than either monotherapy in patients with Crohn's disease (CD). The difference in endoscopic remissiona rates between ABBV-466 and monotherapy groups further increased at Week 24. The findings are from the TARGET-CD study, an ongoing open-label, treat-through, Phase 2a platform study in patients with moderate to severe CD.1,2 The findings will be presented as a late-breaking abstract at the ongoing 2026 Annual United European Gastroenterology Week (UEGW) Congress in Barcelona, October 17–20.


"ABBV-466 reflects how we are building the next generation of our inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) portfolio, leveraging insights from our own research to address disease pathways that may remain active even when a central inflammatory pathway is inhibited," said Kori Wallace, M.D., vice president, global head of immunology clinical development, AbbVie. "Our research pointed to evidence of α4β7-driven inflammation despite risankizumab's IL-23 p19 inhibition, leading us to augment risankizumab with a novel α4β7 inhibitor, trosunilimab. The TARGET-CD results reinforce our strategy of advancing therapies designed around the complex biology of Crohn's disease."


The TARGET-CD study included 300 patients (94, 100, and 106 patients in the anti-IL-23 p19 (risankizumab), anti-α4β7 (trosunilimab), and ABBV-466 treatment groups, respectively) with moderately to severely active Crohn's disease across the spectrum of disease severity and prior treatment experience. While 25% of patients were biologic-naïve, 75% had failed at least one advanced therapy, including 9.3% who had failed prior IL-23 therapy and 12% who had failed a JAK inhibitor; 25% had failed three or more advanced therapies. This patient population reflects the real-world complexity of Crohn's disease, where heterogeneous disease biology can contribute to differences in treatment response across patients.1


At Week 12, 30.2% of patients treated with ABBV-466 achieved the primary endpoint of endoscopic remissiona, compared to 21.3% and 18.0% of patients receiving anti-IL-23 p19 monotherapy and anti-α4β7 monotherapy, respectively. An improvement with ABBV-466 was also reported at Week 24, with 40.5% of ABBV-466 treated patients achieving endoscopic remissiona, compared to 22.4% and 20.0% of patients on risankizumab and trosunilimab monotherapy, respectively.1


Based on gene expression analyses, ABBV-466 showed colonic epithelial repair and barrier restoration at Week 12, followed by tissue remodeling and metabolic changes at Week 24 that were generally not observed with either monotherapy.1


"Many patients with Crohn's disease move from one advanced therapy to the next and still have active inflammation in the bowel, even when their symptoms improve," said Remo Panaccione, M.D., Professor of Medicine and Director of the Inflammatory Bowel Disease Unit, Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology, University of Calgary. "Endoscopic remission is a goal we aim for, because ongoing inflammation can drive disease progression over time. What stands out in the TARGET-CD Phase 2a study is that a dual-targeting approach reached that goal more often than either therapy alone in a heavily pretreated population."


Rates of serious adverse events (SAEs) for ABBV-466 were 10.4% and comparable to risankizumab monotherapy (9.6%) and trosunilimab monotherapy (9.0%). In the ABBV-466 and trosunilimab monotherapy arms, the most common adverse events (≥5%) were Crohn's disease and nausea. In the risankizumab monotherapy arm, the most common adverse events (≥5%) were Crohn's disease and arthralgia.1


Additional information about the program can be found on clinicaltrials.gov under the identifier[NCT06548542](https://edge.prnewswire.com/c/link/?t=0&l=en&o=4800226-1&h=871789670&u=https%3A%2F%2Fclinicaltrials.gov%2Fstudy%2FNCT06548542%3Fcond%3DCrohn%2520Disease%26term%3DNCT06548542%2C%2520TARGET%2520CD%26viewType%3DCard%26rank%3D1&a=NCT06548542) .

**About TARGET-CD** TARGET-CD (NCT06548542) is an ongoing open-label, treat-through Phase 2a platform study in patients with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease. Patients were randomized 1:1:1 to receive 24 weeks of ABBV-466, risankizumab or trosunilimab. The primary endpoint was endoscopic remissiona at Week 12. Additional prespecified endpoints were assessed at Weeks 12 and 24, with safety assessed through Week 24. SES-CD is an assessment tool used during colonoscopy to measure the severity of inflammation and damage in patients with Crohn's disease.


**About ABBV-466** ABBV-466 is an investigational dual-targeting therapy combining risankizumab, an IL-23 inhibitor, with trosunilimab, an α4β7 inhibitor, to address complementary drivers of inflammation in Crohn's disease. The approach is designed to inhibit inflammatory signaling while limiting immune-cell trafficking to the gut, with the goal of achieving deeper disease control than either pathway alone.


ABBV-466 is investigational, and its safety and efficacy have not been established by regulatory authorities.


**EU Indications and Important Safety Information about SKYRIZI** **®** **(risankizumab)** **3**


**Indications**
Skyrizi (risankizumab) is indicated for the treatment of moderate to severe plaque psoriasis in adults who are candidates for systemic therapy.


Skyrizi is indicated for the treatment of moderate to severe plaque psoriasis in children and adolescents from the age of 6 years who are candidates for systemic therapy.


Skyrizi, alone or in combination with methotrexate (MTX), is indicated for the treatment of active psoriatic arthritis in adults who have had an inadequate response or who have been intolerant to one or more disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs).


Skyrizi is indicated for the treatment of adult patients with moderately to severely active Crohn's disease who have had an inadequate response to, lost response to, or were intolerant to conventional therapy or a biologic therapy.


Skyrizi is indicated for the treatment of adult patients with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis who have had an inadequate response to, lost response to, or were intolerant to conventional therapy or a biologic therapy.


**Important Safety Information** Risankizumab is contraindicated in patients hypersensitive to the active substance or to any of the excipients, and in patients with clinically important active infections (e.g., active tuberculosis).


Risankizumab may increase the risk of infection. In patients with a chronic infection, a history of recurrent infection, or known risk factors for infection, risankizumab should be used with caution. Treatment with risankizumab should not be initiated in patients with any clinically important active infection until the infection resolves or is adequately treated.


Patients treated with risankizumab should be instructed to seek medical advice if signs or symptoms of clinically important chronic or acute infection occur. If a patient develops such an infection or is not responding to standard therapy for the infection, the patient should be closely monitored and risankizumab should not be administered until the infection resolves.


Prior to initiating treatment with risankizumab, patients should be evaluated for tuberculosis (TB) infection. Patients receiving risankizumab should be monitored for signs and symptoms of active TB. Anti-TB therapy should be considered prior to initiating risankizumab in patients with a past history of latent or active TB in whom an adequate course of treatment cannot be confirmed.


Prior to initiating therapy with risankizumab, completion of all appropriate immunizations should be considered according to current immunization guidelines. If a patient has received live vaccination (viral or bacterial), it is recommended to wait at least 4 weeks prior to starting treatment with risankizumab. Patients treated with risankizumab should not receive live vaccines during treatment and for at least 21 weeks after treatment.


Serious hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported with use of risankizumab. If a serious hypersensitivity reaction occurs, administration of risankizumab should be discontinued immediately and appropriate therapy initiated.


The most frequently reported adverse reactions were upper respiratory infections (13% in psoriasis, 15.6% in Crohn's disease and 26.2% in ulcerative colitis).


Commonly (≥ 1/100 to < 1/10) reported adverse reactions included tinea infections, headache, pruritus, rash, eczema, fatigue, and injection site reactions.
